newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-BHP says steel market may be worse.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-BHP says steel market may be worse.

text.p: Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd managing director John Prescott said on Tuesday that the trading conditions in the world steel market could be deteriorating.
Asked if the global steel market was getting better, Prescott told Reuters: "No is the short answer. In fact they may even be getting worse."

"Having said that I think prices in the international market are a bit better than what they were in the early months of this year," said Prescott after giving a speech to the Business Council of Australia's annual microeconomic reform conference in Sydney.
Asked if steel margins were improving, Prescott replied: "Yes, but not by much. It is a long tough slog."
In June, BHP said its steel division expected margins to remain under pressure for some time.

Prescott said BHP, Australia's only primary producer of steel, sells 30 percent of its steel to southeast Asia, 30 percent to northeast Asia, 30 percent to North America and 10 percent to the rest of the world.
BHP Steel's profit for the 1995/96 year fell 75.9 percent to A$153 million due to sluggish domestic demand and lower prices.
Prescott said the world steel market was suffering from "inventory issues", new production and structural change in Japan, with Japanese manufacturing industry moving offshore.

"So the demands from the Japanese steel industry at home is not as sustainable as it was once and then offshore those Japanese steel consuming industries are either choosing to buy from Japanese producers or from international producers."
"In our region of the world, the situation has probably been driven by those forces and by fluctuations in business conditions in China that are not notoriously rapid," he said.
Prescott said he could not comment on BHP's trading results for the first three months to August 31, 1996.
But he added the high Australian dollar was still affecting profits. He said a one U.S. cent movement in the Australian dollar affects BHP's bottom-line profit by A$40 million.
The Australian dollar has risen to around US$0.80 currently from $0.73 at the start of 1996.
Prescott said BHP was getting on top of costs at its steel operations. "We are gradually getting on top of some of the cost issues in steel," he said.
Prescott said production at BHP's steel and petroleum divisions were continuing to increase.
"We are seeing a continuation of high levels of production in steel and in petroleum," Prescott said.
At 12.50 p.m. (0250 GMT), BHP shares were 14 cents lower at A$16.70. It hit a high of A$16.96 in earlier trade.
